title: CENTCOM Stands Up Multinational Attack Drone Task Force as US-Iran War Reshapes Unmanned Warfare
subhead: US Central Command launched Task Force Falcon Strike, its first multinational one-way attack drone force spanning air, sea and underwater domains, while Patriot makers slow a Ukraine production deal and the UAE moves to upgrade its THAAD batteries.

sections.heading: Task Force Falcon Strike: CENTCOM's First Multinational Attack Drone Force
sections.body:
US Central Command announced it will stand up Task Force Falcon Strike, its first multinational force built around one-way attack drones operating from above, on and below the sea, according to a CENTCOM release reported by Defense News. The unit, led by personnel from US Special Operations Command Central, will integrate unmanned systems from US forces and regional partners into what CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper called a 'unified multi-domain, multinational deterrent.'

Falcon Strike expands on Task Force Scorpion Strike, established in December 2025, which was the first to launch an aerial attack drone from a US Navy warship and deployed one-way unmanned systems during Operation Epic Fury and strikes on Iranian port facilities in July. The new task force formalizes the shift toward partner-integrated drone warfare in the Middle East, though CENTCOM did not specify which regional partners are involved.
sections.whyItMatters: This institutionalizes the lesson of the Iran war: cheap one-way attack drones are now a core joint capability, and the US is moving from fielding them unilaterally to building a multinational network around them.

sections.heading: Patriot Makers Hedge on Ukraine Production as Competition Fears Surface
sections.body:
Lockheed Martin and Raytheon have begun slowing a joint-production deal to build Patriot interceptors in Ukraine, months after President Trump pledged Kyiv a license at the July NATO summit in Ankara, Defense News reports. A Republican official on Capitol Hill told The Atlantic the real concern is that Ukraine's partners could 'outbuild' the US giants and cut into their monopoly on antiballistic capability, with the companies publicly framing their hesitation around IP theft and tech transfer instead.

The backdrop is a booming Ukrainian defense industry and a US Patriot inventory drained by the Iran war — an estimated two-thirds of pre-war interceptor stock has been expended. Lockheed has meanwhile unveiled the cheaper PAC-3 ACE interceptor at roughly $2 million a round, and Ukraine, nine European countries and firms including Eurosam, Leonardo, Thales and Saab launched the Freyja antiballistic system coalition built around a Ukrainian interceptor priced at about one-fifth of a Patriot round.
sections.whyItMatters: The hold-up reveals the tension between Washington's political pledge to license Patriot production and the commercial interest of US defense primes in protecting a high-margin monopoly — a dynamic that could reshape who builds Western missile defense.

sections.heading: UAE Moves to Upgrade THAAD With New Configuration 3 Launchers
sections.body:
The US Missile Defense Agency awarded Lockheed Martin Space a $211.4 million modification to manufacture new THAAD launchers in Configuration 3 for the United Arab Emirates under the Foreign Military Sales program, per a contract notice published August 13 and reported by Army Recognition. The modification, designated P00082, raises the contract's cumulative value to $1.054 billion and covers production between August 2026 and January 2031.

Configuration 3 is tied to THAAD System Build 5.0, a modernization effort the MDA says is intended to replace obsolete equipment, address cybersecurity vulnerabilities and improve modularity and interoperability, including Link 16 interface updates. Abu Dhabi already operates two THAAD systems as the upper tier of a layered network that also includes Patriot interceptors, giving the Gulf state one of the region's most capable ballistic missile defenses.
sections.whyItMatters: The upgrade signals Gulf states are hardening their upper-tier missile defenses as the Iran war and Houthi drone and missile attacks keep regional air-defense demand high — and it keeps Lockheed's THAAD line funded through the early 2030s.

sections.heading: US Army Puts Next-Generation Armor in Soldiers' Hands: M1E3 and XM30
sections.body:
The US Army's 1st Armored Brigade Combat Team, 1st Cavalry Division — the Iron Horse Brigade — will receive four M1E3 Abrams tank prototypes and rival XM30 infantry fighting vehicle prototypes by the end of 2026 for operational evaluation, Army Recognition reported, citing a Breaking Defense interview with brigade commander Col. Todd Hertling at the GVSETS symposium. The M1E3 is a fundamentally redesigned Abrams with a hybrid-electric engine that cuts fuel demand by 50 percent and an unmanned turret that reduces crew from four to three.

The XM30 competition pits General Dynamics Land Systems' Wolf against American Rheinmetall's Lynx-derived design, with a possible Army down-select in spring 2027 to replace the M2 Bradley. Both prototypes feature remotely operated turrets with 50mm cannons, active protection and open-systems architecture.
sections.whyItMatters: Putting prototypes in an operational brigade rather than keeping them in engineering trials marks a shift toward soldier-driven development, and the XM30 winner will set the technical baseline for US mechanized infantry for decades.

sections.heading: US Army Unveils First Production Maneuver Support Vessel for Indo-Pacific Logistics
sections.body:
Vigor Marine Group presented USAV Craney Island, the US Army's first production Maneuver Support Vessel Light, at its Vancouver, Washington shipyard on August 11, Army Recognition reported. The 117-foot landing craft, designed with BMT, can carry up to 82 tons at 21 knots and reach 30 knots empty, with a draft of about 1.2 meters that lets it approach beaches and shallow coastal waters inaccessible to larger logistics ships.

The vessel is slated for assignment to US Army Pacific, and the shipyard is now in full-rate production of MSV(L) hulls under a contract with a ceiling value of $979.79 million dating to 2017. The program replaces the aging Landing Craft Mechanized 8 fleet and is a centerpiece of the Army's watercraft modernization for distributed operations.
sections.whyItMatters: The MSV(L) reflects the Army's pivot to island-hopping logistics in the Indo-Pacific, where moving heavy armor without major port infrastructure is a core operational problem.

sections.heading: Russian Air Bridge to the Sahel Persists, C4ADS Analysis Finds
sections.body:
Russian state-aligned military forces relied on at least 75 flights by military and military-linked aircraft touching Mali, Burkina Faso or Niger between January 2025 and July 2026, according to a Center for Advanced Defense Studies analysis of ADS-B data reported by Defense News. Burkina Faso received the most flights at 56, followed by Mali at 38 and Niger at six.

The busiest operator was Flight Unit 224, a Russian Defense Ministry-owned airline sanctioned by the US in May 2023, while the Russian Special Flight Squadron conducted 14 flights and the Emergency Situations Ministry 12. C4ADS flagged several private carriers it says remain unsanctioned despite documented links to Russian military logistics, including Kyrgyzstan-registered Sapsan Airlines, and noted growing traffic through Togo and Algeria.
sections.whyItMatters: The sustained air bridge shows Russia is deepening its military logistics network across the Sahel even as Western attention focuses on the Iran war, extending Moscow's reach into West Africa through both state and shadow carriers.

sections.heading: Lockheed's Next Generation Interceptor Passes Stage 2 Rocket Motor Test
sections.body:
Lockheed Martin successfully tested the Next Generation Interceptor's Stage 2 rocket motor under high-vacuum conditions replicating low-Earth orbit, the company announced August 10, Army Recognition reported. The test reduces a key propulsion risk for the future US homeland missile-defense interceptor, which must deliver reliable thrust outside the atmosphere to engage long-range ballistic missiles during their midcourse phase.

NGI is being developed as the future interceptor for the Ground-Based Midcourse Defense system, the principal US architecture for defending the homeland against long-range ballistic missile threats. The data gathered will inform the final interceptor design and accelerate integration with GMD.
sections.whyItMatters: The milestone keeps the homeland missile-defense modernization on track at a moment when the Iran war has highlighted the limits and cost of intercepting ballistic missiles, and when US interceptor stockpiles are under strain.

bottomLine: The defining development of the day is institutional, not tactical: CENTCOM's Task Force Falcon Strike formalizes multinational, multi-domain attack-drone warfare as a standing capability born from the Iran war. Around it, the defense industry is moving on several fronts — US primes are guarding their missile-defense monopolies even as they hedge on licensing production to Ukraine, Gulf states are hardening their THAAD layers, and the US Army is pushing next-generation armor and logistics into operational hands. The through-line is a war-driven acceleration of unmanned systems, missile-defense replenishment and force modernization that shows no sign of slowing even as US-Iran diplomacy pauses strikes.
sources: Defense News, CENTCOM, Army Recognition, Breaking Defense, The Atlantic, C4ADS, Missile Defense Agency, Vigor Marine Group, Lockheed Martin
